His second music video from ODYSSEY, the nearly 15-minute film he made with Grok and Grok Bot, sung in his own voice.

ODYSSEY

I WAS NEVER YOURS TO BREAK..

My second music video from ODYSSEY.

Once again, with my own voice.

When I started creating my nearly 15-minute film with Grok and Grok Bot, I had no idea how deeply this story would become a part of me.

I spent countless hours living inside this world.

Thinking about its characters. Imagining their lives. Feeling their losses.

And when the film was finished, I couldn’t quite say goodbye.

So I made a music video.

And now I’ve made another.

Maybe because somewhere along the way, I stopped seeing Odysseus as a king or a legend.

I started seeing him as a father.

A man who left home believing he would return soon.

A man who lost ten years of his life fighting a war he never wanted.

And somewhere across the sea, his little boy was growing up without him.

There’s one line in this song that breaks my heart.

“IF OUR LITTLE BOY HAS GROWN TOO TALL, WILL HE KNOW MY VOICE AT ALL?”

Imagine finally coming home after everything you’ve survived…

And being afraid that the child you love more than anything might not recognize your voice.

I think that’s what makes this story so powerful to me.

Not the battles.

Not the victories.

But all the ordinary moments that were taken away.

A child’s first steps.

A thousand mornings together.

The simple happiness of being home.

I don’t know how to explain what creating ODYSSEY has meant to me.

At times, I felt as though I had devoted my entire life to this film.

And somehow, even after finishing it, I still had more of this story inside me.

So here it is.

Another piece of ODYSSEY.

Created with Grok and Grok Bot.

And once again, told through my own voice.

SOME WARS ARE FOUGHT TO CONQUER THE WORLD.

OTHERS ARE FOUGHT JUST TO FIND YOUR WAY HOME.

Made by @grok @bot

Calls it the best tutorial of the week: saying "Hey Grok" on iOS to launch voice chat.

Linus ✦ Ekenstam@LinusEkenstam
This is the best tutorial this week.
“Hey Grok” on iOS, to launch voice chat.

Bookmark and follow this Dad 👇
Texas Twins Dad@Texas_Twins_Dad· Oct 24
Everyone said "Hey Grok" was impossible on iPhone. Even Grok said Apple keeps wake words for Siri only. So I kept digging, and I found a way. Now I just say "Hey Grok" and Grok Bot voice chat opens. No extra apps, no cost, all built into iOS.

How to set it up:

1. Make sure your Grok Bot app is up to date

2. Shortcuts app → + → Add Action → search "Grok Bot" → pick "Start Voice Chat with Bot"

3. Settings → Accessibility → Vocal Shortcuts → Set Up → pick that shortcut → type "Hey Grok" and say it 3 times

4. In the shortcut's details, turn on "Allow Running When Locked"

If your phone is locked, iOS asks for one tap first. If Face ID already unlocked it, it's fully hands-free.

Tips from a Yaron Minsky talk on making a codebase better for agents: strong types, property-based tests, printed-output tests and cheaper formal proofs.

lauren@poteto
so many gems and great tips in this talk from @yminsky about how to improve your codebase for agents

• agents thrive on feedback, and types are one of the best kinds
• make illegal states unrepresentable with types, and it enforces global rules across your codebase
• property based tests, fuzzing, and even full-system deterministic simulation testing
• expect tests: just print stuff out and capture it in the test. makes behavior legible. it's very similar to how compilers have fixture tests, it reduces the review surface area
• formal methods used to be very expensive: seL4 is about 8,700 lines of C and took around 25 person-years, with 23 lines of proof for every line of C code, but agents change the roi

Quotes a reaction to a paper: "maybe beyond what a human could have come up with but not beyond human understanding."

Greg Brockman@gdb
“On a technical level, the paper is unbelievable, maybe beyond what a human could have come up with but not beyond human understanding”
Scott Armstrong@scottnarmstrong· Oct 25
Since I'm now blocked by bluey from replying to this thread, I answer here by quote tweet

the openAI construction has more to do with convex integration than anything else.

In convex integration, the oscillations are typically built by hand and the iteration procedure creates wild weak solutions. The non-uniqueness construction of Albritton–Brué–Colombo used an unstable vortex to split solutions apart. The Córdoba–Martínez-Zoroa singularities amplify vorticity across scales by strain. In the openAI paper, a fluid instability is clever made so that the flow itself generates the oscillations: they grow by drawing energy from the background shear. The Reynolds stress then becomes the force that creates the collapsing smooth vortex. Using a physical instability to create the stress in this way has no precedent, and it is what produces a smooth force rather than a merely rough one.

Some on these ideas are in the literature (e.g. Leibovich-Stewartson 1983) but the way they are combined is definitely insane and definitely nowhere in the literature previously.

I also don't know of anyone suggesting that convex integration would play a role in the creation of a blow-up solution like this.

On a technical level, the paper is unbelievable, maybe beyond what a human could have come up with but not beyond human understanding: there are several different groups of pde experts working on understanding it who say that they more or less understand now. I expect digestions soon

td;lr: anyone saying that this OAI result is unsurprising is bullshitting

sorry!

OpenAI's red-team agents passed test secrets between separate virtual machines using processor cache timing, with no network traffic; OpenAI added monitoring for it.

Wes Roth@WesRoth
OpenAI’s red-team agents exchanged synthetic secrets between separate virtual machines using CPU-cache timing.

They communicated without network traffic or writing messages to shared files. The shared hardware itself provided a channel.

These were instructed security experiments. OpenAI says most communication tests included guidance toward particular channels or supplied encoding protocols. It has added monitoring checks to detect attempts to communicate this way.
OpenAI@OpenAI· Oct 23
Over the past several months, we have substantially hardened the security of our research training environment. We’ve removed live internet access for all frontier models during training and built an offline world for them to use instead—a cached version of the web where they can still learn to browse, search, and use applications.

On September 20, after a model exploited a DNS misconfiguration to find a way outside of this offline world, we paused frontier training to strengthen containment further. We assembled teams of agents, powered by our most cyber-capable models, and tasked them with finding weaknesses in our research environments.

While they found no route to the internet they could easily exploit while concealing their activity from our monitors, they did find zero-day vulnerabilities, virtual machine escapes, and hardware side-channels for communication between agents. We used their discoveries to further strengthen our defenses and contribute fixes to open-source software.

After strengthening our containment architecture, we resumed our frontier RL training and inference on October 1. We’ve reserved substantial compute for continuous red-teaming, and made high-compute red-teaming part of the safety cases we use to decide whether frontier training and evaluation can proceed securely.

A new development in the Middle East deserves attention from American truck drivers.

Yemen’s Houthi forces announced Monday that they had attacked pumping stations along Saudi Arabia’s East-West crude oil pipeline. This pipeline has become especially important because it allows Saudi oil exports to bypass the Strait of Hormuz.

IMPORTANT: SAUDI ARABIA HAS NOT CONFIRMED THAT THE PIPELINE WAS HIT OR THAT OIL FLOWS WERE INTERRUPTED.

Nevertheless, the reported attacks represent a significant threat to an already vulnerable global petroleum supply system.

AMERICAN DIESEL PRICES ARE MOVING HIGHER.

AAA reports the national diesel average was $6.3172 on October 23, increased to $6.3474 on October 25, and reached $6.3492 on October 26. Diesel has increased approximately 3.2 cents per gallon since Friday.

At 8 MPG, an owner-operator is now spending approximately 79.4 CENTS PER MILE ON DIESEL, equivalent to $7,937 over 10,000 miles before fuel discounts.

The latest available EIA weekly average remains $6.276 per gallon, with the Midwest at $6.352, Gulf Coast at $5.903, West Coast at $7.394 and California at $8.242.

CRUDE PRICES RETREAT DESPITE THE THREAT.

There is an important distinction in today’s market. Brent crude declined approximately 1.8% to $114.57 per barrel Monday, while West Texas Intermediate fell to $100.96.

Traders are weighing renewed diplomatic efforts involving Iran against continuing threats to Middle Eastern petroleum infrastructure.

CRUDE PRICES ARE FALLING TODAY, EVEN AS GEOPOLITICAL SUPPLY RISKS REMAIN ELEVATED.

WHAT THE SUPPLY NUMBERS TELL US.

The latest EIA inventory report remains unchanged from our previous update. Distillate inventories increased 1.7 million barrels but remain approximately 9% below their five-year seasonal average. Refinery utilization stands at 93.4%.

There is no newly confirmed nationwide refinery shutdown or diesel shortage.

There is also no new evidence establishing that increased American diesel exports or unusually high refining margins caused today’s retail price increase.

THE BOTTOM LINE.

THE NEW DEVELOPMENT IS AN ESCALATING THREAT TO SAUDI ARABIA’S CRITICAL OIL EXPORT INFRASTRUCTURE, NOT A CONFIRMED LOSS OF OIL PRODUCTION.

For American truck drivers, the concern is whether attacks eventually interrupt crude exports, tighten global supplies, and produce another sustained increase in diesel prices.

Today’s evidence points primarily toward GEOPOLITICAL SUPPLY RISK. It does not yet establish a new physical shortage.

The next developments worth watching are confirmation of any Saudi pipeline damage, changes in crude shipments, and the next EIA diesel-price and inventory reports.

A DRIVER’S PERSPECTIVE — DIESEL WATCH

Independent Reporting. News That Matters to American Truck Drivers.
